title: Terraform in Production: Modules, State and Teams
subtitle: Reusable modules, safe state, tested pipelines and Kubernetes add-ons
description: Take Terraform from a personal tool to a team platform: write versioned modules, store state remotely with locking, refactor safely, test and scan code, deploy through OIDC-authenticated pipelines and manage Kubernetes add-ons.
outcomes: Design, version and consume reusable modules
Run remote state with locking and environment isolation
Refactor and repair state with moved, import and removed blocks
Ship Terraform through tested, keyless CI/CD and manage Kubernetes with it

lessons.title: Writing reusable modules
lessons.summary: Design modules with a clear contract: typed inputs, minimal outputs, pinned providers and composition.
objectives: Explain root versus child modules
Write typed, validated variables and focused outputs
Structure a module repo with examples and tests
Compose two module calls by passing outputs

sections.title: What you will build and the path through this course
sections.body:
In this course you move from "I can run `terraform apply` on my laptop" to running Terraform as a team in production. You will build a small, versioned module library, store state remotely with locking, recover from broken state, test and scan your code, ship it through a CI pipeline that authenticates to AWS without stored keys, and finally manage Kubernetes objects and Helm releases from Terraform.

The path: **(1) module design** (this lesson), **(2) module sources, the registry and versioning**, **(3) remote state and environment isolation**, **(4) state surgery** with moved/import/removed blocks, **(5) testing and policy**, **(6) CI/CD and secrets**, **(7) Kubernetes with Terraform and safe refactors**. Each lesson assumes the previous one. This course expects Terraform 1.6 or newer, the AWS provider 5.x, and the basics from Terraform Essentials: resources, variables, outputs, plan and apply.

A **module** is simply a directory of `.tf` files that you call from another configuration. Every Terraform configuration is already a module (the **root module**); modules you call are **child modules**. Modules are how you stop copy-pasting the same VPC or cluster definition between environments.

sections.title: About this example: a module directory layout
sections.body: This is the conventional layout of a reusable module in its own repository. You do not run it; it shows which file holds what. Look at `variables.tf` and `outputs.tf`: together they are the module's public interface, while everything else is implementation that callers should never depend on.

sections.title: terraform-aws-network/ (layout)
sections.code:
terraform-aws-network/
├── main.tf          # resources (aws_vpc, aws_subnet, ...)
├── variables.tf     # inputs: the module's parameters
├── outputs.tf       # outputs: what callers can read
├── versions.tf      # required_version + required_providers
├── README.md        # usage example, inputs/outputs table
├── examples/
│   └── basic/main.tf  # runnable example, also used in tests
└── tests/
    └── basic.tftest.hcl
sections.note: Name repositories terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> so the public registry can index them later.

sections.title: About this example: typed inputs with validation
sections.body: The next file declares the module inputs. Each variable has a type, a description and, where sensible, a `validation` block that fails the plan early with a readable message. Look at `cidr_block` (validated with `can(cidrnetmask(...))`) and `azs` (a list with a sane default is deliberately not given, so callers must choose).

sections.title: modules/network/variables.tf
sections.note: Prefer precise types (object({...}) with optional()) over `any`; they document intent and catch typos.

sections.title: About this example: calling the module and reading outputs
sections.body: This root configuration calls the module twice with different inputs, which is the whole point of reuse. You run it with `terraform init` and `terraform plan`. Notice `module.network_prod.vpc_id`: callers read only declared outputs, never inner resources.

sections.title: envs/main.tf (calling a module)
Module design rules of thumb
head: Rule
Why
Example
rows: Every input is API you must keep stable
Fail at plan, not at apply
No provider blocks in child modules
Deep trees are hard to reason about
Root calls `network` and `cluster`, passes ids between them

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Wrapper modules** that just re-expose one resource with 40 passthrough variables add cost, not value. **Hard-coding** region, account ids or names inside a module makes it unusable elsewhere. **Putting `provider` blocks** in a child module blocks `count`/`for_each` on the module and complicates removal. **Outputs of whole resources** leak internals; output specific attributes.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
A module is a directory with an input/output contract. Design it small: typed and validated variables, minimal outputs, pinned provider constraints, an `examples/` directory and no provider blocks. Compose modules in the root by passing outputs of one as inputs of another.

Next lesson covers where modules live: local paths, Git tags and the Terraform Registry, plus how to version and consume them safely.

questions.question: Which file(s) form a module's public interface?
questions.explain: Inputs and outputs are what callers depend on; resources are internal.

questions.question: Why avoid provider blocks inside child modules?
options: They make the module hard to reuse and block count/for_each and clean removal
questions.explain: Providers should be configured in the root and passed in; embedded providers couple the module to one configuration.

questions.question: What does a variable validation block do?
options: Rejects bad input at plan time with a custom message
questions.explain: validation conditions are evaluated during plan, giving early readable errors.

lessons.title: Module sources, registry and versioning
lessons.summary: Consume modules from local paths, Git and registries with pinned versions, and upgrade them without surprises.
objectives: Choose between local, registry and Git sources
Write correct version constraints
Use for_each on modules
Upgrade a module and review the plan

sections.title: Where modules come from
sections.body:
Terraform resolves the `source` argument of a module call at `terraform init` and copies the module into `.terraform/modules`. Sources can be a **local path** (`./modules/x`), a **registry address** (`terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws`), a **Git URL** pinned by tag (`git::https://...?ref=v1.2.0`), or an object-storage archive. Only registry sources support the `version` argument; for Git you pin with `?ref=`.

Because modules are code you execute with cloud credentials, you must treat them like dependencies: pin exact or tightly bounded versions, review upgrades, and prefer sources you trust.

sections.title: About this example: version constraints and source types
sections.body: This file shows the same module consumed three ways. The registry call uses `version = "~> 5.8"` (any 5.x at or above 5.8), the Git call pins an immutable tag with `?ref=`, and the local call has no version at all. Read the comments, then run `terraform init` to see each one downloaded.

sections.title: main.tf (three module sources)
sections.note: Pin Git sources to a tag or commit SHA, never to a branch.

sections.title: About this example: what terraform init prints
sections.body: Running `terraform init` downloads every module and provider and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`. Look at the lines for each module (registry version resolved, Git ref cloned) and the provider selection; commit the lock file so everyone gets identical provider builds.

sections.title: About this example: upgrading a module safely
sections.body: The sequence below upgrades a registry module: raise the version constraint, run `terraform init -upgrade`, then read the plan carefully. Focus on lines marked `must be replaced`, which indicate that the new module version would recreate a resource.

sections.title: Upgrade and inspect the diff
sections.code:
sed -i 's/~> 5.8/~> 5.13/' main.tf
terraform init -upgrade
terraform plan -out=upgrade.tfplan | tail -n 8
sections.output:
Plan: 0 to add, 3 to change, 0 to destroy.

Changes to Outputs:
  ~ vpc_arn = "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:vpc/vpc-0a1b2c3d4e" -> (known after apply)

Saved the plan to: upgrade.tfplan

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Unpinned Git branches** (`?ref=main`) make plans non-reproducible. **`version = ">= 5.0"`** will happily jump a major version. **Ignoring the plan after an upgrade**: a module bump can replace NAT gateways or databases. **Copying a registry module's code** into your repo loses security updates; fork only with intent.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Modules come from local paths, registries or Git; pin them tightly, commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`, and read the plan after every upgrade. Use semantic versions (major for breaking changes, with `moved` blocks for renames) for your own releases.

Next: where Terraform keeps its memory. We move state to a remote backend with locking and split it per environment.

questions.question: What does version = "~> 5.8" allow?
questions.explain: The pessimistic operator allows increments of the last specified part: >= 5.8, < 6.0.

questions.question: How do you pin a Git module source?
questions.explain: The version argument is only for registries; Git uses ?ref=.

questions.question: Why commit .terraform.lock.hcl?
options: It records exact provider versions and hashes for reproducibility
questions.explain: The lock file makes all machines and CI use identical providers.

lessons.title: Remote state and environment isolation
lessons.summary: Configure an S3 backend with locking, keep one state per stack and choose an environment-separation strategy.
objectives: Create a secure S3 state bucket
Configure the S3 backend with native or DynamoDB locking
Migrate local state to a backend
Compare workspaces, directories and Terragrunt

sections.title: Why state must be remote
sections.body:
Terraform's **state** file maps your configuration to real resources and stores their attributes. Locally it lives in `terraform.tfstate`, which is fine for one person and dangerous for a team: it is easy to lose, to overwrite concurrently, and it may contain secrets. A **backend** stores state remotely and, ideally, takes a **lock** so two applies cannot run at once.

The standard AWS setup is an **S3 bucket** (versioned, encrypted, private) as backend. Since Terraform 1.10 the S3 backend supports **native locking** with `use_lockfile = true`, which writes a `.tflock` object next to the state; the older approach uses a **DynamoDB table** with a `LockID` key. New setups should prefer native S3 locking; DynamoDB locking is deprecated but still works.

sections.title: About this example: bootstrapping the state bucket
sections.body: This small configuration creates the bucket once, with versioning (so you can roll back state), default encryption and public access blocked. Apply it with local state first, then never touch it casually; the bucket name is globally unique, so change it. Look at `versioning_configuration` which is your safety net.

sections.title: bootstrap/main.tf
sections.note: The bootstrap bucket is the one resource you cannot store in the backend it creates; keep its tiny state in the repo or recreate it by import.

sections.title: About this example: the S3 backend block
sections.body: Each environment gets its own `key` (state path). `use_lockfile = true` enables S3 native locking; the commented DynamoDB line is the legacy alternative. Backend blocks cannot use variables, so pass differing values with `-backend-config` or keep one file per environment, as this example does.

sections.title: envs/prod/backend.tf
About this example: migrating local state to the backend
sections.body: After adding the backend block, `terraform init -migrate-state` offers to copy your existing state. The answer `yes` uploads it. Afterwards the local file is empty and plans read from S3; the lock appears while an apply runs.

sections.title: Three ways to separate environments
head: Approach
How
Strength
Weakness
rows: `terraform workspace new prod`; same code and backend, `terraform.workspace` selects values
Same credentials and bucket; easy to apply to the wrong workspace; not for prod isolation
envs/dev, envs/prod each with own backend key and tfvars, calling shared modules
Explicit, separate blast radius, different accounts possible
Wrapper that generates backends and DRY-s inputs across directories
Removes boilerplate, dependency graph between stacks

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **One giant state** for everything: slow plans and a huge blast radius; split by lifecycle and ownership (network, cluster, apps). **Using workspaces for prod versus dev** in one account and bucket. **Disabling locking** with `-lock=false` to get past an error instead of finding who holds the lock. **State bucket without versioning**, leaving no way back after a bad apply.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Store state in a versioned, encrypted, private S3 bucket with native locking (or DynamoDB on older versions), one key per stack and environment. Prefer directory-per-environment for strong isolation; use workspaces for short-lived copies and Terragrunt when boilerplate hurts.

Next: what to do when state and reality diverge, from renames with `moved` to recovering a stuck lock.

questions.question: What does use_lockfile = true do in the S3 backend?
options: Enables native S3 state locking via a .tflock object
questions.explain: Terraform 1.10+ can lock using S3 conditional writes, removing the DynamoDB requirement.

questions.question: Which is the main weakness of workspaces for production isolation?
options: They share the same backend and credentials, so mistakes cross environments
questions.explain: Workspaces separate state files only; access control and blast radius stay shared.

questions.question: Why enable versioning on the state bucket?
options: To recover an earlier state after corruption or a bad apply
To allow variables in backend blocks
questions.explain: Each state write creates a version you can restore.

lessons.title: State surgery: moved, import and removed
lessons.summary: Refactor safely with declarative state changes and recover from locks and corrupted state.
objectives: Rename and relocate resources with moved blocks
Adopt existing resources with import blocks
Forget resources with removed blocks
Release a stale lock and restore a previous state

sections.title: Why state surgery exists
sections.body:
Refactoring code changes addresses. If you rename `aws_instance.web` to `aws_instance.app`, Terraform sees one resource gone and a new one wanted, so it plans a destroy and create. **State surgery** tells Terraform "these are the same object" without touching the real infrastructure. Since 1.1 you do this declaratively in code with `moved` blocks; since 1.5 `import` blocks, and since 1.7 `removed` blocks. The older CLI commands (`terraform state mv`, `rm`, `import`) still exist for one-off fixes.

Declarative blocks are preferred because they are reviewed in a pull request, planned like any change, and apply identically for every teammate and environment.

sections.title: About this example: a moved block
sections.body: This file renames a resource and moves another into a module. Terraform reads each `moved` block during plan and updates the state address, so the plan shows `has moved to` instead of destroy and create. Keep the block in your code until all environments have applied it.

sections.title: refactor.tf
sections.note: Never delete a moved block that other environments have not applied yet.

sections.title: About this example: import and removed blocks
sections.body: An `import` block adopts an existing resource into state at the next apply; `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` can even draft the resource body for you. A `removed` block with `destroy = false` forgets a resource without deleting it, useful when handing ownership to another team.

sections.title: adopt.tf
About this example: recovering a stuck lock
sections.body: If an apply is killed (CI cancelled, laptop closed), the lock may remain. The error names a lock `ID` and who holds it. Confirm nobody is actually running, then release it with `force-unlock`. With S3 native locking you can also delete the `.tflock` object.

sections.title: Lock error and release
sections.code:
terraform plan
terraform force-unlock 3f1c2b9e-77a4-5c1d-9b0e-1a2b3c4d5e6f
sections.output:
Error: Error acquiring the state lock

Lock Info:
  ID:        3f1c2b9e-77a4-5c1d-9b0e-1a2b3c4d5e6f
  Path:      acme-tfstate-123456789012-us-east-1/prod/network/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       ci@runner-42
  Created:   2026-11-13 09:14:02 UTC

Terraform state has been successfully unlocked!

sections.title: Which tool for which situation
head: Situation
Preferred tool
Notes
rows: Rename resource or move into module
`aws s3api list-object-versions`, copy back, `terraform state push` last resort
Only after confirming no run is active

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Editing the state JSON by hand** without a backup and without bumping the serial. **`force-unlock` while an apply is really running** can corrupt state. **Removing a `moved` block too early** so other environments plan a destroy. **`terraform state rm` followed by apply** when the resource is still in code: Terraform will try to create it again and fail on the name conflict.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Use `moved`, `import` and `removed` blocks for refactors, keep CLI surgery for emergencies, always back up state first, and rely on bucket versioning for recovery. Locks are released with `force-unlock` only after you verify no run is active.

Next: raise the quality bar with automated tests, linters, security scanners and policy as code.

modules.title: Quality, delivery and Kubernetes
modules.summary: Testing, pipelines, secrets and cluster add-ons.

lessons.title: Testing, linting and policy as code
lessons.summary: Add terraform test, tflint, security scanning, pre-commit and policy-as-code checks to your workflow.
objectives: Write and run terraform test files
Configure tflint and a security scanner
Wire checks into pre-commit
Explain OPA and Sentinel policy enforcement

sections.title: Quality gates for infrastructure code
sections.body:
Infrastructure changes can delete databases, so you want automatic checks before a human reviews a plan. A practical pipeline layers: **formatting** (`terraform fmt`), **validation** (`terraform validate`), **linting** (`tflint`, finds invalid instance types and deprecated syntax), **security scanning** (`checkov` or `trivy config`, the successor to tfsec), **tests** (`terraform test`), and **policy** (OPA or Sentinel) over the plan.

Run the cheap checks first and locally through **pre-commit** hooks, then repeat them in CI where they cannot be skipped.

sections.title: About this example: a native terraform test
sections.body: Files ending in `.tftest.hcl` are run by `terraform test` (Terraform 1.6+). This test uses `command = plan` so it creates nothing, then asserts on planned values. Look at the `run` block, its `variables` and each `assert` with a readable message.

sections.title: tests/basic.tftest.hcl
sections.note: Use command = apply tests only in a sandbox account; Terraform destroys what the test created afterwards.

sections.title: About this example: security scanning and pre-commit
sections.body: Checkov scans Terraform for misconfigurations such as unencrypted buckets. The output lists failed checks with resource and file lines. The second file wires fmt, validate, tflint and checkov into pre-commit so problems are caught before you commit.

sections.title: Scan with checkov
sections.code: checkov -d . --framework terraform --quiet --compact
sections.output:
Passed checks: 41, Failed checks: 2, Skipped checks: 0

Check: CKV_AWS_18: "Ensure the S3 bucket has access logging enabled"
	FAILED for resource: aws_s3_bucket.assets
	File: /main.tf:12-18

Check: CKV_AWS_145: "Ensure S3 bucket is encrypted with KMS by default"
	FAILED for resource: aws_s3_bucket.assets
	File: /main.tf:12-18

sections.title: About this example: pre-commit hooks
sections.body: This `.pre-commit-config.yaml` is not a Kubernetes manifest, so it is shown as text. Install with `pre-commit install`; hooks then run on staged files at every commit. Pin each `rev` to a release tag.

sections.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml
sections.code:
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform
    rev: v1.96.1
    hooks:
      - id: terraform_fmt
      - id: terraform_validate
      - id: terraform_tflint
      - id: terraform_checkov
        args: ["--args=--quiet"]
      - id: terraform_docs

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Only scanning in CI**, so developers learn about failures late. **Blanket skips** (`#checkov:skip`) without a written reason. **Tests that apply into production accounts.** **Unpinned tool versions**, making pipelines flaky when a scanner adds rules.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Layer cheap to expensive: fmt, validate, tflint, checkov, terraform test, then policy over the JSON plan. Run them in pre-commit and again in CI.

Next: wire these checks into a delivery pipeline: plan on pull request, apply on merge, and no long-lived AWS keys.

lessons.title: CI/CD, OIDC and secrets for Terraform
lessons.summary: Build a plan-on-PR, apply-on-merge pipeline that authenticates to AWS with OIDC and no stored keys.
objectives: Explain plan on PR and apply on merge
Keep secrets out of code and protect them in state
Create an OIDC provider and scoped trust policy
Write a GitHub Actions workflow with gated apply
Describe the Atlantis workflow

sections.title: The delivery model: plan on PR, apply on merge
sections.body:
A safe Terraform workflow mirrors application CI. On every **pull request** the pipeline runs fmt, validate, lint and scans, then `terraform plan` and posts the plan as a comment so reviewers see exactly what will change. After merge to the main branch, the pipeline runs `terraform apply` of **the same saved plan** (or a fresh plan gated by approval). Humans review the plan; machines apply it.

Two security rules matter most: the pipeline must not hold **long-lived AWS access keys**, and the role used for pull request plans should be **read-only** while only the main branch can assume the write role.

sections.title: About this example: OIDC trust in AWS
sections.body: GitHub Actions can obtain short-lived AWS credentials through OpenID Connect. This HCL registers GitHub as an identity provider and creates an apply role whose trust policy accepts only tokens from one repository and branch. The `sub` condition is the critical line: widen it carelessly and any repo could assume the role.

sections.title: iam-oidc.tf
sections.note: Create a second role trusted for pull_request events with read-only permissions for plans.

sections.title: About this example: GitHub Actions workflow
sections.body: This workflow is a GitHub file, not a Kubernetes manifest, so it is shown as text. Jobs request `id-token: write` to mint the OIDC token, assume the role with no stored secrets, run checks, and plan on pull requests. The apply job runs only on `main` and uses an environment with required reviewers.

sections.title: .github/workflows/terraform.yml
sections.code:
name: terraform
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  plan:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: 1.10.5 }
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/terraform-plan
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan

  apply:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: 1.10.5 }
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/terraform-apply
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform apply -input=false -auto-approve
sections.note: -auto-approve is acceptable only because the environment gate and the PR review already approved the change.

sections.title: About this example: secrets and least privilege
sections.body: This file shows three habits. A `sensitive` variable is redacted from plan output (but still stored in state, so the state bucket must be encrypted and locked down). The password is generated and written to Secrets Manager rather than committed. The IAM policy gives the plan role read access to the state object only. Atlantis users declare the same roles in `atlantis.yaml` projects.

sections.title: security.tf
sections.note: Anything Terraform writes into a resource is in state in plain text, even if marked sensitive. Ephemeral resources (Terraform 1.10+) keep values out of state.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Static access keys in CI secrets.** **Trust policy with `sub` of `repo:acme/*`** which lets every repo apply. **Planning in the PR and re-planning at apply** so the applied change differs from the reviewed one. **No concurrency control**, allowing two pipelines to compete for the lock; use a `concurrency` group per stack.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Plan on PR with a read-only OIDC role, apply the reviewed plan on merge with a separate write role, and keep no static keys anywhere. Atlantis offers the same flow driven by PR comments. Mark secrets sensitive, generate them instead of committing them, encrypt state and grant each role the minimum IAM actions.

Next: protecting secrets and permissions, then bringing Kubernetes under Terraform control.

options: Credentials are short-lived and tied to repo and branch claims

lessons.title: Managing Kubernetes with Terraform, drift and refactors
lessons.summary: Use the kubernetes, helm and kubectl providers without ordering traps and handle drift and big refactors safely.
objectives: Choose between the kubernetes, helm and kubectl providers
Configure providers so cluster creation and use do not collide
Install a chart with helm_release
Detect and resolve drift and plan large refactors

sections.title: Terraform and Kubernetes together
sections.body:
Terraform is a good fit for the **platform layer** (the cluster, node pools, IAM, namespaces, and installing controllers with Helm) and a poorer fit for fast-moving application manifests, which are often better handled by GitOps. Three providers matter: **kubernetes** (native resources such as namespaces and ConfigMaps), **helm** (`helm_release`, installs Helm 3 charts) and **kubectl** from the community (`kubectl_manifest`, applies arbitrary YAML including CRDs without needing the schema at plan time).

The central pitfall is **provider configuration ordering**: the kubernetes and helm providers need the cluster endpoint and credentials, but those only exist after the cluster resource is created. If the cluster and the workloads live in the same state and the providers read attributes of a not-yet-created cluster, the first plan fails or targets the wrong cluster.

sections.title: About this example: provider configuration from a cluster data source
sections.body: This file configures the kubernetes and helm providers using values from the cluster. The `exec` block runs the AWS CLI to fetch a short-lived token at each run, so no kubeconfig or static token is stored. Check that the data source reads an existing cluster; that is why a separate stack for workloads is safest.

sections.title: providers.tf
sections.note: Best practice: stack 1 creates the cluster, stack 2 (this one) installs add-ons. Never create the cluster and configure these providers from it in one apply.

sections.title: About this example: a namespace and a helm_release
sections.body: This sample creates a namespace with the kubernetes provider and installs ingress-nginx with `helm_release`. The `values` list holds YAML as a string, `atomic = true` rolls back a failed upgrade, and `depends_on` ensures the namespace exists. These are the same chart concepts as helm install, driven from state.

sections.title: addons.tf
sections.note: Always pin `version`; an unpinned chart upgrades silently on the next apply.

sections.title: About this example: applying and checking from both sides
sections.body: After `terraform apply`, verify with helm and kubectl: Terraform owns the release, so `helm list` shows it as deployed, and the pods run in the namespace. The output shows revision 1 and ready replicas.

sections.title: Apply and verify
sections.code:
terraform apply -auto-approve
helm list -n ingress-nginx
kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx

sections.title: Drift and large refactors
head: Situation
Command or practice
Notes
rows: Shows differences between state and reality without changing config
Use when a manual change is intended; then update the code
Exit code 2 means drift; alert on it
Split into small PRs with `moved` blocks
Plan must show no destroys before applying
Back up state, apply to dev first, use `-target` only for recovery
Targeted applies leave config and state inconsistent
On databases, clusters and state buckets

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **Cluster and workloads in one apply** with providers configured from the new cluster. **Unpinned Helm chart versions.** **Mixing owners**: Terraform and Argo CD or `kubectl apply` fighting over the same objects, causing permanent drift. **Large `-target` workflows** that hide dependency problems. **Giant refactors in one PR** instead of a series of reviewable steps.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Use Terraform for the cluster and platform add-ons, configure the kubernetes and helm providers in a separate stack from the cluster, pin chart versions and let a single tool own each object. Detect drift with refresh-only plans and refactor in small steps using `moved` blocks.

You have now covered module design, versioning, remote state, surgery, quality gates, secure pipelines and Kubernetes management. A natural next step is the Amazon EKS course, where these patterns create real clusters.

questions.question: Why keep cluster creation and add-on installation in separate stacks?
options: Providers need cluster attributes that do not exist until the cluster is created
questions.explain: Provider configuration is evaluated before resources exist, causing ordering problems.

questions.question: What does helm_release atomic = true do?
options: Rolls back automatically if the install or upgrade fails
questions.explain: Atomic upgrades roll back on failure.

questions.question: Which command shows drift without proposing config changes?
questions.explain: refresh-only compares state with reality.
